title: A spliceosome-independent eukaryote generated by complete intron removal

verified.what_i_actually_checked: I queried NCBI BioProject PRJNA1157626 and the matching ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) file report: it contains exactly 25 public sequencing runs and nothing else - 15 RNA-seq (messenger RNA sequencing) runs covering 5 strains (SY14, SYNE21, SYNE24, SYNE26, SYNE27) at 3 replicates each, plus 10 whole-genome sequencing runs (Illumina and PacBio). I summed the reported base counts (121.9 Gbp) and the per-run FASTQ byte sizes (~48 GB of compressed raw reads). I confirmed there is no GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) series, no processed count matrix, and no supplementary file reachable through Europe PMC (the article has no PubMed Central ID; the one PMC link NCBI returned, PMC13591232, is an unrelated review).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything biological: the 300 deleted spliceosomal introns, the slow-growth phenotype, ribosomal dysregulation, recessive fitness cost in diploids, and the dispensability of the five small nuclear RNAs and of Prp8/Prp9/Prp19/Yhc1/Luc7. All of this comes from the abstract and press releases. The full text and the supplementary tables are behind Elsevier's paywall (cell.com returned HTTP 403), so I could not see any table of per-intron coordinates, growth rates or differential-expression results.

a1_downloadable.note: The only public deposit is raw sequencing in the Sequence Read Archive (25 runs, ~48 GB of FASTQ). Every processed, model-ready table lives in the paywalled Cell supplement: cell.com returns HTTP 403 and there is no PubMed Central copy, so I could not open a single analysis-ready file.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No label column exists anywhere in the public data. Any target - per-gene expression change on intron removal, or per-intron fitness cost - would have to be built from scratch by aligning and quantifying raw reads, then computing differential expression myself. This is exactly the 'you have to construct the thing you are predicting' failure.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs would be fine if a label existed: the Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome and all 300 intron sequences are freely available from SGD (Saccharomyces Genome Database), so no thousands of identifier lookups are needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Nothing to state units for. There is no measurement table in the public release; read counts are not an outcome in stated units, and the growth-rate and expression units used in the paper are only visible in the inaccessible supplement.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified in ENA: the biological unit is the strain, and there are 5 strains with 3 replicates = 15 RNA-seq samples. Even the most generous framing (one row per spliceosomal intron) caps out at ~300 rows, under the ~400-row floor for classification and far under ~1,500 for regression.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~48 GB compressed FASTQ (121.9 Gbp of reads) across 25 runs
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified by summing ENA fastq_bytes. This is raw sequencing data, which this project explicitly never downloads, and it is roughly ten times the ~5 GB working-set limit. Alignment is CPU-feasible for yeast but the download and the tens of CPU-hours are not.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not checkable. The paper's own tables are paywalled, so I cannot compare the claimed 300 introns or any sample count against the deposited files beyond confirming 25 SRA runs exist.

a8_label_provenance.note: Undeterminable, and that is the problem. Because no label is published, whatever label I built would be my own pipeline's output (my aligner, my differential-expression call), so the model would partly be learning my preprocessing rather than a measured quantity.

existing_models.name: Deep learning intron-structure classifier of gene essentiality (Life Science Alliance 2021, e202000951; found via web search, abstract snippet only, full paper not retrieved)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported AUC (area under the receiver-operating curve) 0.857 classifying essential vs non-essential genes from intron sequence alone, per the search snippet; split not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not verified - I did not retrieve the discussion section.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 (DNA language models) would have been the natural fit for intron sequence features
backbone.hardware: CPU, since ~300 intron sequences is a trivial embedding job
backbone.licence: Permissive for both (not relevant here, since there is no label to fit a head to)

integration.partner_dataset: SGD (Saccharomyces Genome Database) intron annotations plus the yeast deletion-collection fitness data
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which sequence or expression features of an intron predict whether removing it costs the cell fitness? - a good question, but this paper contributes 5 strains and no per-intron outcome table, so the join adds nothing that SGD and the older single-intron-deletion studies do not already provide.

controls.positive_control: Would have been: recover the known textbook result that ribosomal protein genes are intron-enriched and most intron-sensitive. Not runnable without a per-intron outcome.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling - not applicable, there is no label.
controls.external_validation: Parenteau et al. single-intron-deletion fitness measurements in yeast exist as an independent source, but they are the data one would actually model, not this paper.

honest_claim_h3: With 5 strains and 15 RNA-seq samples and no published outcome table, no model trained on this paper's public data could claim anything beyond a description of five specific laboratory strains.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an intron's DNA sequence and position to predict how much removing it harms yeast growth.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one spliceosomal intron of Saccharomyces cerevisiae: its sequence, length, position within the gene, and the host gene's expression level. At most ~300 examples exist in this organism, and this paper publishes no outcome value for any of them.
plain_idea.predict: The fitness or expression cost of deleting that intron. The true answer would have to come from growth-rate measurements or RNA sequencing of intron-deletion strains - this paper made only 5 cumulative-deletion strains, so there is no per-intron measurement to learn from.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Synthetic-genome groups minimising eukaryotic genomes would want to know which introns are safe to delete before building a strain. Even a failed model would tell them that intron sequence alone does not predict deletion tolerance.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper adds 15 RNA-seq samples across 5 strains. The 2021 intron-structure essentiality classifier used genome-wide intron sets across species; our contribution would be smaller, not bigger.

confidence_score.why: Three replicates per strain gives a noise estimate for 5 conditions only, which is nowhere near enough groups to calibrate per-prediction confidence over ~300 introns.

models_beatable.why: The one model I found is from 2021 and predicts gene essentiality from intron sequence, which is a different and easier target than deletion fitness cost; I could not verify its split or whether its weights are public.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on the first condition: there is no baseline model for this exact task that I could run, and no new data here that measures the same quantity the same way, because this paper measures no per-intron quantity at all.

ml_idea: The project considered was: predict, for each of the ~300 yeast spliceosomal introns, the fitness or expression cost of deleting it, from intron sequence features plus a DNA language-model embedding. It dies because this paper publishes only 5 cumulative-deletion strains and no per-intron outcome; the per-intron labels one would need come from older single-deletion studies, not from here.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed. The 48 GB working set and ~40 hours are the download-plus-alignment-plus-quantification cost of 121.9 Gbp of raw reads, which I computed from the ENA file report. RAM and model-fitting costs are small only because the final table would have at most a few hundred rows - which is the reason to reject, not a reason it is cheap.

verdict_reason: Five Part A killers fail. Verified in the repositories: the only public data is 48 GB of raw sequencing (25 runs, 15 RNA-seq samples from 5 strains, 10 whole-genome runs), there is no processed table and no outcome column anywhere, the Cell supplement that would hold one is paywalled (HTTP 403, no PubMed Central copy), and the biological unit count is 5 conditions - or at most ~300 introns - against a floor of 400. This is a landmark biology result built on a single engineered strain; it is not an ML dataset.
